description: Question: steel, aluminium and titanium are about equally stiff for their weight, so why are airframes aluminium and carbon-fibre composite, and why were early aircraft and gliders made of spruce? Idea: the Ashby chart and material performance indices. On log axes of Young's modulus E against density ρ, a design's best material lies along lines of constant index: E/ρ for a tie or strut in tension (mass ∝ ρ/E), E^½/ρ for a beam in bending (mass ∝ ρ/E^½), E^⅓/ρ for a plate or panel in bending (mass ∝ ρ/E^⅓). Data: Wikidata's SI-normalized values (psn:), so a value typed in MPa or g/cm³ lands in Pa and kg/m³: 35 engineering materials with a recorded tensile modulus (P5480) and density (P2054), and 405 elements and minerals with bulk (P5668) and shear (P5673) moduli, whose Young's modulus follows from isotropic elasticity, E = 9KG/(3K+G), with Poisson's ratio ν = (3K−2G)/(2(3K+G)). A sanity check sets aside 2 rows (A36 steel at 0.2 GPa, MPa typed for GPa; PET at 1.38 kg/m³, g/cm³ typed for kg/m³). What it shows: for a tie, steel (26.8 MJ/kg), aluminium 6061-T6 (25.6) and titanium (24.8) are the same, so a tie of aluminium weighs 1.05× the steel one. For a beam it weighs 0.60× and for a panel 0.50×: the cube root forgives aluminium's low stiffness while its low density counts in full. Further up the panel ranking: magnesium 0.35×, carbon-fibre polyamide 0.34×, beryllium 0.21×, and white spruce 0.15×, the best of all 438 materials as a panel. Caveats: a small crowd-curated sample; the K and G values carry no reference and look computed (DFT-like: identical numbers for all silica polymorphs, G > K for silica, magnesium's E 60 GPa against a handbook 45), and where both exist they differ from the recorded E by 5–37% (titanium, molybdenum, rhodium); pure elements are not alloys; polycrystal averages hide anisotropy, and wood and fibre composites are stiff only along the grain; stiffness only (strength, toughness, fatigue, cost and joining ignored). Next: strength indices σ^(2/3)/ρ for panels that must not yield, AFLOW's DFT elastic constants for thousands of crystals, why lithium (top 3 here) goes into Al-Li airframe alloys.
name: Ashby chart: why aircraft are aluminium, CFRP and spruce
